finding.claim: The /settings/email endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. Authentication is not enforced on a state-changing account operation. Depending on set_email's implementation, this could update a row with a NULL or None uid, or fail with an unhandled error. It is also the wrong control: the sibling /settings/password endpoint uses @login_required. Email change is typically the first step of an account takeover through password reset.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated remote client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie.
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which modifies an account's email address.

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when no session exists, and never aborts.
The route is registered with methods=['POST'] and decorated with @login_optional.
set_email(g.uid, ...) runs with g.uid possibly None and no authentication check.
By contrast, /settings/password uses @login_required, which shows the intended control.

finding.guards_checked: Checked for an auth check inside change_email and found none. login_optional does not abort. There is no CSRF protection and no re-authentication or current-password check on the route. set_email is a stub (line 48), so the real impact depends on its implementation, but the missing authentication is on the route itself. The app also sets no secret_key in this file, so session handling is configured elsewhere.
